chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Ali ibn Abi Hamza, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

I asked him (peace be upon him) about when the walking of the walker should cease. He (peace be upon him) said: 'When he pelts the Jamarat al-Aqaba and shaves his head, then his walking has ceased, so let him visit (the Kaaba) riding.'

key_terms.جَمْرَةَ الْعَقَبَةِ: The largest pillar of the Jamarat in Mina, where pilgrims throw pebbles on the 10th of Dhu al-Hijjah
key_terms.حَلَقَ رَأْسَهُ: Shaving the head, a key ritual act concluding the major rites of Hajj
key_terms.رَاكِباً: Riding (on a mount), indicating the permission to use transport after the specific rites
key_terms.مَشْيُ الْمَاشِي: The walking of the pilgrer, referring to the ritual of walking to the Kaaba

ai.seo_question: When does the obligation to walk to the Kaaba end during Hajj?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi clarifies the transition from the ritual of walking (Mashi) to riding (Rakub) during Hajj, specifically linking the end of the walking obligation to the completion of the stoning of Jamarat al-Aqaba and the shaving of the head. In Shia jurisprudence, this highlights the distinction between the initial approach to Mecca and the subsequent rites, emphasizing that once the major pillars of Hajj are performed, the pilgrim may utilize transport for the remaining Tawaf. This ruling underscores the flexibility within the ritual structure, allowing for ease once the core obligations are fulfilled.
